stops.title: Göbekli Tepe: monuments before farming
stops.blurb: On a hilltop in southeastern Turkey, people began raising rings of carved limestone pillars around 9600 BCE. The tallest stand over five metres, and many carry animals in relief. The builders were hunter-gatherers who had not yet domesticated plants or animals. The excavators think people gathered here to feast, and perhaps to drink beer brewed from wild grain.
stops.debate: The excavators see the circular buildings as special places for ritual and feasting; Banning argues they may have been large houses rich in symbolic art.

stops.title: The first farmers of southwest Asia
stops.dateNote: Cultivation and herd management began by about 9500 BCE; domestic forms took one to two thousand years more to become clear.
stops.blurb: In an arc of hills from the Levant through southeastern Turkey to the Zagros mountains of Iran, people tended wild cereals and managed wild herds for centuries before these changed into domestic forms. Wheat, barley, lentils and peas, then goats, sheep and cattle, were domesticated in different parts of the arc. It was a slow process spread over a whole region, not a single invention.

stops.title: Farming begins again and again
stops.dateNote: The map shows each centre from its earliest good evidence, between about 9500 and 3000 BCE.
stops.blurb: Farming was not invented once and then spread. It began separately in at least eleven regions, with different plants and animals: wheat and goats in southwest Asia, millet and rice in China, taro and bananas in New Guinea, squash, maize and manioc in the Americas, sorghum in Africa. The dates differ by thousands of years, and the earliest farmers in each place had no contact with the others.

stops.title: Jericho and Çatalhöyük: the first big villages
stops.blurb: Farming let villages grow large. At Jericho, beside a spring in the Jordan valley, people built a stone wall and a tower 8.2 metres high between about 8300 and 7800 BCE. At Çatalhöyük in Turkey, from about 7100 BCE, several thousand people lived in mud-brick houses packed so tightly there were no streets. People walked across the roofs and climbed down into their homes.
stops.debate: Kathleen Kenyon read Jericho's wall as a defence against attackers; Bar-Yosef argued it was built in stages against floods and mudflows.

stops.title: Millet, rice and the first wine in China
stops.blurb: In northern China, people at Cishan were storing broomcorn millet between about 8300 and 6700 BCE, East Asia's first dry-land crop. Further south, rice changed slowly: plants whose ripe grains stay on the stalk, a sign of domestication, were still increasing around 4900 to 4600 BCE. At Jiahu, residues in pottery show a fermented drink of rice, honey and fruit by about 7000 BCE.

stops.title: Squash, maize and manioc in the Americas
stops.blurb: Farming in the Americas began with squash. Seeds from Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca, Mexico, show domesticated squash between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago. Maize was growing in Mexico's Central Balsas valley by about 6700 BCE. In South America, people in the Bolivian Amazon grew manioc and squash more than 10,000 years ago, and early gardens in northern Peru held squash, peanuts and cotton.

stops.title: What farming cost
stops.dateNote: Farming began at different times in different places, so these changes are spread over thousands of years.
stops.blurb: Farming fed more people, but the bones of early farmers show a price. In most regions studied, adults grew shorter as farming took hold. Crowded villages, living beside their animals and rubbish, suffered more infections, and grain-heavy diets brought tooth decay. Families had more children, so populations grew fast. Over the long run, gaps in wealth between households widened.

stops.title: Mehrgarh: barley, zebu and the first dentists
stops.dateNote: Gangal and colleagues date the earliest farming levels as early as 8500 BCE; the drilled teeth are 9,000 to 7,500 years old.
stops.blurb: At Mehrgarh, at the foot of the hills of Baluchistan in Pakistan, villagers grew mostly barley with some wheat and kept zebu, the humped cattle of South Asia. Barley and zebu were probably domesticated locally; the wheat came from southwest Asia. Nine adults buried here had molars drilled while they were alive, between 9,000 and 7,500 years ago, the oldest known dentistry.

stops.title: Farmers move into Europe, and start milking
stops.blurb: Farming reached Europe with farmers. Ancient DNA shows that the first farmers across Europe descended mainly from people of the Aegean and western Turkey. Between about 7000 and 4000 BCE they spread along the Mediterranean by boat and up the Danube into central Europe. They brought cattle, and fats in their cooking pots show milk use by the seventh millennium BCE.

stops.title: The sea drowns Doggerland
stops.blurb: As the ice sheets melted, the sea rose over the low plain that had joined Britain to the rest of Europe. By about 6200 BCE only low coast and islands were left. Then an undersea landslide off Norway, the Storegga slide, sent a tsunami across the North Sea. Seabed cores show it struck the coast, but the land recovered for a while before rising seas covered it.
stops.debate: The tsunami was long thought to have ended Doggerland at a stroke; Gaffney, Walker and colleagues argue its effects were local and that rising sea level finished the job later.

stops.title: Fire that makes metal
stops.blurb: For thousands of years people had hammered lumps of natural copper into beads. Smelting is a different skill: heating ore until the metal runs out of the rock. Slag from Belovode in Serbia shows copper was being smelted there by about 5000 BCE, around the time cast copper tools appear in the Balkans. Metal objects became prized goods that travelled far.
stops.debate: Radivojević and colleagues see Belovode as evidence that smelting was invented in more than one place; Roberts and colleagues argue for a single invention in southwest Asia in the early sixth millennium BCE.

stops.title: The green Sahara dries out
stops.blurb: For thousands of years after the ice age the Sahara was wetter, with grassland and lakes where there is desert today. Herders kept cattle there, and fats in their pottery show they were milking them in the fifth millennium BCE. As the summer monsoon weakened, the land dried. Lake sediments in Chad show trees, then grass, disappearing, and today's desert in place by about 700 BCE.
stops.debate: A dust record off West Africa suggests the wet period ended abruptly about 3500 BCE; lake sediments in Chad show a gradual drying, and a later synthesis finds the end came progressively later further south.

stops.title: Tombs of giant stones
stops.blurb: In the second half of the fifth millennium BCE, people in northwest France began building tombs from huge stones, or megaliths. Radiocarbon dates suggest the idea then spread by sea along the Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts within a few centuries. The tradition lasted two thousand years. At Stonehenge in England, a circular ditch and bank came about 3000 BCE, and the great stones about 2500 BCE.
stops.debate: Schulz Paulsson's dates point to an origin in northwest France and spread by sea; an older view holds that megaliths arose separately in several regions.

stops.title: The horse and the wheel
stops.dateNote: The earliest wheeled vehicles are dated to the later fourth millennium BCE in both Europe and Mesopotamia.
stops.blurb: Around 3500 BCE, people of the Botai culture in Kazakhstan kept horses: wear from bridles and traces of mare's milk in pots show some were harnessed and milked. Yet ancient DNA shows today's domestic horses descend from a later population near the Volga and Don rivers. Wheeled wagons appear in central Europe and Mesopotamia at about the same time as Botai.
stops.debate: Botai's horses turn out to be ancestors of Przewalski's horses, not of modern domestic breeds, so where and when horses were first tamed for riding is still argued over.

p: From about 9600 BCE, on a limestone ridge near the modern city of Şanlıurfa in southeastern Turkey, people built a series of round and rectangular enclosures. Each was ringed by T-shaped stone pillars, cut from the bedrock nearby and set upright, with two larger pillars in the middle. The tallest are over five metres high. Many are carved with animals in relief. Some have arms, hands and belts carved on their sides, which suggests they stood for human-like beings. Building went on, on and off, until about 8200 BCE.

The animal bones come from wild species, mostly gazelle, so the builders lived by hunting and gathering. Radiocarbon dates place the oldest enclosures before the first domesticated crops and animals in the region. Large limestone vessels and the pattern of animal bones led the excavators to propose that people met here in large numbers to feast, and that beer brewed from wild grain may have been part of it.

The excavators long called Göbekli Tepe a sanctuary, a place for ritual rather than daily life, and newspapers turned that into "the world's first temple". UNESCO uses more careful language. In 2011 the archaeologist Edward Banning argued that the buildings might have been houses, large and full of symbols, like the decorated houses of later villages such as Çatalhöyük. He pointed out that art does not by itself make a building religious. The excavators replied that the special buildings are the rule at the site, not the exception. How many people lived there all year, and how the work of moving the pillars was organised, are still open questions.

The usual story was that farming came first, and that villages, surplus food and big monuments followed. Göbekli Tepe turns part of that around. Hunter-gatherers here organised the labour to quarry, carve and raise huge stones, at about the time their neighbours began cultivating wild cereals. The excavators think that gatherings like these, which needed lots of food in one place, may have been one of the pressures that pushed people toward farming. Whether or not that is right, the site shows that complex shared beliefs and big projects did not wait for agriculture.

Between about 9500 and 3000 BCE, people in many parts of the world began to cultivate plants and keep animals, each group working with what grew around them. Researchers count at least eleven regions where farming started independently, and several more have been suggested.

In southwest Asia it was wheat, barley, lentils and peas, with goats, sheep and cattle. In northern China, broomcorn millet was being stored at Cishan by about 8300 to 6700 BCE, and rice was slowly domesticated along the Yangtze. In the highlands of New Guinea, people at Kuk Swamp were clearing forest and tending plants by about 8000 BCE and growing bananas in mounds by about 5000 BCE. In Mexico, squash was domesticated by 8,000 years ago and maize by about 6700 BCE. In the Bolivian Amazon, manioc and squash were grown more than 10,000 years ago. In eastern North America, squash, sunflower and two seed plants called marshelder and chenopod were domesticated from about 5,000 years ago. In eastern Sudan, pottery from about 3500 to 3000 BCE carries the imprints of domesticated sorghum.

Domestication leaves marks on plants and animals. Wild cereals scatter their seeds when ripe; domesticated ones keep them on the stalk until harvest, and the break left on the grain shows which kind it was. Squash seeds and stalks grow larger. Starch grains and tiny silica bodies called phytoliths survive on tools and in soil long after the plant has rotted. Impressions of chaff in pottery preserve the shape of grain. Radiocarbon dating of the remains themselves gives the timing, and the genes of modern crops point to where their wild ancestors grew.

Two questions run through the field. One is how fast domestication happened. Some once argued it could take as little as a century or two; the archaeological evidence for wheat, barley and rice now points to two to four thousand years of slow change. The other is how to tell an independent centre from a place that received crops or ideas from elsewhere. Genes can flow between crops and their wild relatives, which blurs the trail. Eastern North America was long thought to have borrowed its crops from Mexico before the evidence showed they were local.

Farming began again and again, on different continents with different plants, within a few thousand years after the ice age. It was not one lucky discovery that spread from a single cradle. The crops of these centres still feed the world: wheat, barley, rice, maize, millet, sorghum, squash, bananas and manioc are among them. And because each region started with its own plants and animals, the farming societies that grew from them took different paths, a difference that shaped the rest of history.

Jericho sits beside a large spring on a gentle slope in the Jordan valley. Between about 8300 and 7800 BCE, its early farmers built a stone wall 3.6 metres high around their settlement, and inside it a round stone tower 8.2 metres high, with a staircase of 22 steps inside. The tower weighed around 1,000 tonnes. Later they dug a ditch in front of the wall and added more walls.

About a thousand years later, Çatalhöyük grew up in south-central Turkey. It was lived in from about 7100 to 5950 BCE, and at its height, around 6700 to 6500 BCE, it held between 3,500 and 8,000 people. Mud-brick houses were built wall to wall with no streets between them. People moved across the flat roofs and climbed down into their homes. Many walls inside and out carried paintings and reliefs.

At Jericho, Kathleen Kenyon's excavations cut trenches through the mound and exposed the wall and tower. Radiocarbon dates from those layers give the building dates. At Çatalhöyük, modern excavations have studied the houses layer by layer, and the skeletons found there. The bones record diet, disease, injury and how much people walked. The houses show no buildings much grander than the rest, which suggests a society without strong ranks.

Kenyon saw Jericho's wall as a fortification and estimated that 3,000 to 4,000 people lived inside. In 1986 Ofer Bar-Yosef pointed out that the tower stood inside the wall, where it would be of little use to defenders. He proposed that the wall was built in stages to hold back floods and mudflows from a nearby stream, and estimated the population at 400 to 900. At Çatalhöyük, whether to call the settlement a town, a proto-city or a very large village depends on the definition.

These places show what farming made possible, and what it brought with it. Thousands of people could now live in one place all year. They built together and filled their homes with images. They also lived with crowding: at Çatalhöyük, rubbish pits and animal pens sat beside houses, traces of faeces were found in walls and floors, and healed head wounds became more common when the town was most crowded.

Farming produced more food from each patch of land, and the number of people grew. But for the people who lived through the change, it was not simply an improvement. Early farmers in many regions were shorter than the foragers before them, worked harder, and were sicker. Their villages were crowded, close to their animals and to their own waste. Over the following millennia, farming societies also became more unequal.

The evidence is mostly in bones and teeth. A review of stature studies published since 1984 found that, in most cases, adult height fell as people came to rely on farming. This was seen in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, South America and North America, whenever farming arrived. An earlier survey had found declining health in 19 of 21 societies that made the change.

Çatalhöyük in Turkey gives a close-up view. In a sample of 93 skulls, 25 people had healed fractures, and 12 of them had been hurt more than once; more than half of the victims were women. About 10 to 13 percent of adult teeth had cavities, from a diet heavy in grain. Up to a third of people from the early period show signs of infection on their bones. Leg bones show that later residents walked much further, probably because fields and pastures had moved further away.

Cemeteries around the world also show a sudden rise in the share of young people in the population soon after farming began. Researchers read this as a jump in births, of roughly two more children per woman. Comparing house sizes over time, another team found that differences in wealth generally grew after plants and animals were domesticated, and grew most in Eurasia.

Much of this is inference. The rise in births is read from the ages of skeletons in cemeteries, not counted directly. The pattern is also not the same everywhere: the review of stature found that most, but not all, studies show a decline. Why inequality grew more in Eurasia is argued over. Kohler and colleagues suggest that large domestic animals, such as oxen for ploughing and later horses for warriors, let some households and states grow far richer than others, but this is one explanation among several.
The change to farming is often told as progress. The bones suggest a more mixed story: more people, but harder lives for many of them, and the start of lasting gaps between rich and poor.

Farming came to Europe from southwest Asia, and it came mostly by migration. Between about 7000 and 4000 BCE, farming communities spread from the Aegean and western Turkey into the Balkans, up the Danube into central Europe, and along the Mediterranean coasts by sea, setting up farming settlements on the shore. They brought wheat, barley, sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. Hunter-gatherers already living there sometimes took up the new ways, and sometimes kept to the old ones for centuries.

The farmers also brought milking. Cattle were especially important in northwestern Turkey, and fats from milk turn up in cooking pots there and in southeastern Europe by the seventh millennium BCE. Across Europe, milk use was widespread from then on.

Ancient DNA is the strongest evidence for migration. Genomes of early farmers from northern Greece and northwestern Turkey closely match those of early farmers across Europe, from the Mediterranean to central Europe. The farmers of Europe were their descendants. Radiocarbon dates from early farming sites get younger with distance from southwest Asia, at roughly a kilometre a year on average.

Milk is detected chemically. Animal fats soak into the walls of unglazed pots, and milk fats can be told apart from meat fats by their chemistry. One study of more than 2,200 vessels found milk by the seventh millennium BCE; a later one used about 7,000 residues from more than 550 sites to map milk use across Europe over 9,000 years.

The ability to digest the milk sugar lactose as an adult is called lactase persistence. It depends on a gene variant that is common in Europe today, and the usual explanation was that milk drinkers had an advantage. But the gene variant was rare among early farmers. It appears around 4700 to 4600 BCE and was not common until about 1000 BCE, thousands of years after milk use became widespread. In 2022 Evershed and colleagues found that the amount of milk people used did not explain the rise. They suggest that drinking milk without the gene was mostly harmless, but became dangerous during famine or epidemics, and that this drove the selection. Not every researcher is convinced.

The spread of farming into Europe is one of the clearest cases where an idea travelled because people did. And milk, a food that many adults could not digest, became a staple long before their bodies adapted to it.
